source_document: Document 7 — Chief Justice John Marshall, Worcester v. Georgia, 1832

left.label: In 1832, Chief Justice Marshall ruled that the laws of Georgia “can have no force” on Cherokee land (Doc 7).

right.label: This shows the Supreme Court sided with the Cherokee against a state, which matters because removal went ahead anyway — so the law protected them on paper and not on the ground.

rationale.a: It says what the ruling shows in the student's own words, it says why that matters, and it lands back on the claim that expansion cost people their rights. Notice it does not repeat the quotation.

documents.source_text: . . . The Cherokee nation, then, is a distinct community occupying its own territory, with boundaries accurately described, in which the laws of Georgia can have no force, and which the citizens of Georgia have no right to enter, but with the assent [agreement] of the Cherokees themselves, or in conformity with treaties, and with the acts of congress. . . .
